1.pericope_label: Give the king thy judgments: the prayer for the king and the peace the mountains bring

schools.summary: Augustine holds that what is said here cannot apply to Solomon at all, so that the name is figurative and stands for the true peace-maker.

Calvin argues from the closing subscription that David is the author and that Solomon only versified his father dying prayers, and warns against reading the psalm simply as a prophecy of Christ; Gill names the king as Christ and cites the old synagogue, and collects older readings of the mountains.

Henry applies the prayer first to Solomon as a father blessing and a king prayer for his successor and then to Christ, arguing that a kingdom lasting as long as the sun cannot be Solomon; Spurgeon makes the double reference structural, since both are king and king son.

Clarke surveys the versions on the authorship and settles on David in his last days, and declares the received division of the third verse false and meaningless; Wesley reads the plural judgments as the branches of one office and the mountains as the dangerous places.

Keil and Delitzsch take the prefixed letter as marking authorship and argue from style, geography and the affinity with Job that Solomon wrote it; Ellicott turns the futures into wishes, derives peace as the fruit of righteousness, and notes the missing article.

debates: Who wrote the psalm, and of whom? Keil and Delitzsch take the prefixed letter as marking authorship and find Solomon in the style, the geographic range and the affinity with the Book of Job; Calvin holds the inscription indeterminate, argues from the closing subscription for David, and adds that Solomon could not have praised his own reign without vanity, conjecturing only that he versified his father prayers; Clarke reviews the ancient versions, which divide between the two, and settles on David in his last days.

How far does the psalm reach beyond Solomon? Augustine says nothing here can apply to Solomon at all and takes the name figuratively of the peace-maker, Henry argues that a kingdom lasting as long as the sun cannot be his, and Gill and Spurgeon read the king as Christ throughout, while Calvin warns that reading the psalm simply as a prophecy does violence to the words and gives opponents occasion to object.
outliers: Clarke declares that the received clause about the little hills has no meaning at all, because the verse has been falsely divided, and moves the words in righteousness to the head of the following verse on the authority of the old Greek version.
Calvin cautions against applying to Christ what does not directly refer to him, on the ground that it hands opponents of the faith an occasion to cry out against the whole method.
themes: a prayer for the king and his successor
righteousness as the ground of peace
the poor and needy under royal protection
a kingdom outlasting the sun
the division of the text

5.pericope_label: They shall fear thee as long as the sun endureth: the rain on the mown grass and the dominion from sea to sea

schools.summary: Spurgeon extends the dominion from one ocean to the other and contrasts the greatest earthly emperor with his King, while declining to say whether the universal reign precedes or follows the personal advent.

Gill allows the fear to be either the oppressors or the people of God, collects the ancient renderings of the shorn grass, denies that the dominion can fit Solomon, and reads the flourishing righteous under the figure of the palm that grows under pressure.

Clarke reads the rain as the night dew restoring what the day grazing consumed and measures the dominion by the exact frontiers of Solomon kingdom, yet holds that the fear of this verse can belong to no man at all; Wesley makes God the object of the fear and keeps the river as a border enjoyed by three kings.

Ellicott renders the time phrases literally, refuses to decide whether God or the king is feared, weighs the geography of the dominion against its hyperbole without settling it, and takes the shearing either as a mown field or as grass ready for mowing; Keil and Delitzsch explain both phrases as periphrases for unlimited time.

debates: Who is the object of the fear? Ellicott says the question must remain unanswered, Wesley answers at once for God, Gill allows either the oppressors or the people of God fearing the Messiah, and Clarke holds that there is no sense in which the verse can be spoken of Solomon or of any other man, so that it belongs to Christ alone.

Is the dominion from sea to sea geography or hyperbole? Clarke maps it precisely onto the frontiers of Solomon kingdom while allowing the utmost latitude when the words are referred to Christ, Gill denies it can fit Solomon at all, Spurgeon stretches it from ocean to ocean, and Ellicott weighs the vagueness of the phrase ends of the earth and the hyperbole of the neighbouring verses against the named places that follow, without deciding.
outliers: Clarke supports the picture of the night dew from a Latin poet of husbandry in Dryden version, then supplies the plain prose as well, remarking that poetry always says too much or too little.
Spurgeon expressly refuses to take a side on whether the universal reign of his King comes before or after the personal advent, leaving it for the discussion of others.
themes: fear enduring with sun and moon
rule descending like rain on cut grass
the righteous flourishing under a good reign
the reach of the kingdom
a poetical or a mapped dominion

9.pericope_label: They that dwell in the wilderness shall bow: the kings of Tarshish and Sheba and their gifts

schools.summary: Gill collects the ancient renderings of the desert dwellers and leaves the place name between the sea and a distant western country, and insists that the homage of kings is religious worship due to one equal with the Father.

Clarke prefers coast dwellers living by navigation, denies that the gifts are tribute since Solomon had no jurisdiction in the countries named, and concedes that if the homage is taken of the whole globe it cannot be Solomon at all; Wesley says as much in one sentence.

Ellicott takes the desert dwellers for nomads, reads the presents as the payment of tribute on the strength of the literal phrase, identifies the place with the Tartessus of the Greeks, and divides the other two names between Arabia and Africa; Keil and Delitzsch settle the ambiguous word by context and find men beyond dispute.

debates: Who are those that dwell in the wilderness? Gill and Clarke both report that the ancient versions render it Ethiopians, Clarke preferring coast dwellers who live by navigation and fishing on the strength of another version that gives islands, Ellicott taking them for nomad tribes of the desert, and Keil and Delitzsch ruling that the word covers both beasts and men and that here they are men beyond all dispute.

Are the gifts of the kings tribute or friendly presents? Ellicott renders the phrase as return presents and insists it means payment of tribute, comparing our words revenue and custom-house returns; Clarke denies it outright, since the king had no jurisdiction in the countries named, and takes the words for a grateful offering and a compensative present made on account of benefits received.
outliers: Ellicott divides the two remaining names between the continents, making the Joktanic kingdom of Yemen stand for Arabia and the Cushite one for Africa.
Gill offers as one sense of the place name a large country inhabited by the Celtae, distinct from the islands of the sea.
themes: the desert brought into submission
prostration before a sovereign
tribute or gift from distant kings
the homage of all kings
a claim too large for any earthly reign

12.pericope_label: For he shall deliver the needy when he crieth: the ground of the kingdom in the care of the poor

schools.summary: Spurgeon grounds submission in a condescending rule rather than in dread, makes the bare cry of the needy the most potent of pleas, and inverts the proverb about self-help.

Gill defines the needy as those sensible of their want and turns the deceit and violence inward, to the deceitfulness of sin, the old serpent and false teachers, and to the dominion of sin and the strong man armed.

Clarke keeps the deceit and violence in the courts, where the poor are cheated and the helpless oppressed, and extends the avenging of blood even to a murderer of the blood royal; Wesley calls them the two usual ways of destroying life and makes the king a father who will not be prodigal of his subjects lives.

Ellicott argues from the tense that the wide sway is asked on the strength of a justice already exercised, and notes with Keil and Delitzsch that the verse repeats a line from the book of Job; Keil and Delitzsch make the world dominion the reward of the king condescension.

debates: Why is the dominion of the world asked for this king? Keil and Delitzsch answer that it is the reward of his condescension toward the poor and oppressed, and Ellicott that the verb must be read as a present, so that the petition rests on a justice already shown; Gill and Spurgeon read the same verses as a description of the king character rather than as the ground of the request.

What are the deceit and the violence he redeems from? Clarke and Wesley keep both in the ordinary world of cheated peasants and murdered subjects, with the king justice reaching even the chief in the land, while Gill reads them of the deceitfulness of sin, the old serpent and false teachers, and of the tyranny of sin itself.
outliers: Clarke presses the avenging of blood to its limit, holding that the murderer shall not be screened even if he is of the blood royal.
Spurgeon turns the proverb about God helping those who help themselves the other way round, holding it truer that his King helps those who cannot help themselves nor find help anywhere else.
themes: care of the poor as the ground of empire
the cry that needs no eloquence
deliverance from fraud and force
blood held precious by the king
justice reaching the highest offender

15.pericope_label: And he shall live: the gold of Sheba, the corn upon the mountains, and the enduring name

schools.summary: Spurgeon takes the prayer as offered for his King and grounds it in the church being his body and the truth his sceptre, while allowing that the words may be read as through him.
Gill reads the living either of the redeemed man or of the Messiah, keeps the handful as a figure of small beginnings, and takes the enduring name as a perpetual office rather than a lasting fame.

Clarke explains the prayer from the duties of conquered peoples and contrasts this king with ordinary conquerors, keeps the handful as literal husbandry, and states plainly that a commentator business is the literal and historical sense unless the New Testament directs otherwise; Wesley builds a christological argument on the smallness of the handful.

Ellicott makes the delivered man of the previous verse the one who prays, rejects the rendering that prays to the king, and turns the handful into abundance with the mountains themselves under grain; Keil and Delitzsch derive the same rare word from a root meaning to expand.

debates: Is it a handful of corn or an abundance? Ellicott derives the rare word from a root meaning to spread and renders it abundance, with the mountain woods themselves turned to grain, and Keil and Delitzsch reach the same sense from the Jewish lexicographers; Wesley and Gill keep the handful and build on its smallness an argument that the verse cannot fit Solomon, whose kingdom was as large at the start of his reign as at its end, while Clarke keeps the handful as plain husbandry.

Who prays, and for whom? Ellicott holds the subject to be the poor man protected in the preceding verse, who blesses his benefactor, and calls the rendering that directs prayer to the king inadmissible; Clarke explains it from the obligation of conquered peoples to pray for their conqueror in public worship; Spurgeon reads it as prayer made for his King.
outliers: Clarke states his rule of interpretation at the close of the psalm, that a commentator must find the literal sense and the historical fact and not seek allegories where there is no certain evidence of them, following the New Testament writers only where they lead.
Ellicott hears in the verb rendered wave the language of earthquake and storm rather than of a quiet cornfield, and calls the older versions picture of lowland corn overtopping Lebanon grotesque.
themes: life and gifts returned to the king
prayer offered for or through the king
a handful or an abundance of corn
population springing up like grass
a name that outlasts the sun

18.pericope_label: Blessed be the Lord God: the doxology closing the book and the note that the prayers are ended

schools.summary: Henry makes the thanksgiving rest on the certainty of a word not yet fulfilled; Spurgeon refuses to expound the doxology at all, holding that it is meant for adoration rather than exposition, and reads the closing line as an abdication before the crowned King.

Gill takes the blessing as due to this King by right, reads every name of his as glorious, and offers two accounts of the closing line, either the last psalm written or the last that David himself arranged.

Clarke argues from the miracles that Christ is God, and observes that the apostasy of the son was deliberately hidden from the father, partly in mercy and partly because the matter was still contingent and left to free will; Wesley takes the closing line as plain biography.

Keil and Delitzsch place the blessing as the closing benediction of the second book, explain the divine name used in it from the character of that book, and treat the closing line as the superscription of an older collection and evidence for the history of the Psalter.

debates: What is the closing line, and who set it there? Wesley and Clarke take it as biography, the note of a last psalm, Clarke adding that later pieces of David have got out of their proper connection; Gill allows either that or the close of a collection David himself arranged; Keil and Delitzsch make it the superscription of a primary collection rather than part of the doxology, and argue that since no one surveying the whole Psalter could have set such a keystone here, the line must predate the division into five books.

How much of the future was shown to the psalmist? Henry and Spurgeon treat the prophecy as settled and complete, while Clarke observes that the apostasy of the son was withheld, partly so that the father might die in peace and partly because God would not predict as certain what was still poised between being and not being, the scale left to the free will of the creature.
outliers: Clarke states a doctrine of contingency at the close of the psalm, that God will not predict as absolutely certain what still hangs in the balance, since he leaves the turning of that scale to the free will of his creature.
Spurgeon declines to expound the doxology, quoting an older writer that these verses explain themselves and are meant for adoration rather than exposition.
themes: thanksgiving for a promise not yet fulfilled
the glory of the divine name
what was hidden from the psalmist
the close of a book and of a collection
a king content to subside into nothing
